title: Cross-Border Data Transfer and Significant Data Fiduciary Duties Under the DPDP Rules, 2025
subtitle: What Section 16 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act actually permits, what the 2025 Rules add for a significant data fiduciary, and the compliance clock now running for a foreign company's India subsidiary, GCC or outsourcing vendor
meta_description: DPDP Section 16 cross-border transfer and significant data fiduciary duties under the 2025 Rules, for a foreign company's India entity, as on Nov 2026.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian, Subhradip Roy
author_role: Bhaskar Subramanian, Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Subhradip Roy, Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
seo_title: DPDP Cross-Border Transfer and SDF Rules 2025 Explained
standfirst: A foreign company running an India subsidiary, a global capability centre or an outsourcing arrangement is told, correctly, that India's data protection law lets it move personal data abroad without asking anyone's permission first. That is true as far as it goes, but the 2025 Rules add a second layer that only bites once a company is designated a significant data fiduciary, and the two layers run on different clocks. Getting the timing wrong, treating a 2027 obligation as live today, or an already-live retention duty as something that can wait, is the actual risk.
key_points: Section 16 of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 works as a negative list: a data fiduciary may transfer personal data outside India to any country or territory unless the Central Government specifically restricts that destination by notification, and as on date no country has been so restricted.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, notified in November 2025, stagger commencement across three timelines, and most substantive obligations, including the significant data fiduciary provisions in Rule 13 and the data retention duty in Rule 8(3), come into force eighteen months later, placing the live compliance date around the middle of 2027, not immediately.

Rule 13 restricts a significant data fiduciary, a status the Central Government must expressly confer by notification under Section 10, from moving specified categories of traffic data outside India; as on date the government has not notified any entity as a significant data fiduciary.

Section 16(2) lets a sectoral regulator's stricter data localisation or transfer rule override the Act's permissive default, so a company relying on the negative list cannot ignore RBI payment-data localisation, insurance sector rules or similar sector-specific restrictions that already exist independently of the DPDP Act.

Rule 8(3) requires every data fiduciary, significant or otherwise, to retain personal data together with related traffic data and processing logs for one year, a requirement that sits on the same eighteen-month commencement timeline as the significant data fiduciary provisions.

The Schedule to the Act tiers penalties by the type of default, reportedly up to Rs 250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards, up to Rs 200 crore for a breach-notification or children's-data default, and up to Rs 150 crore for breach of a significant data fiduciary's specific obligations, adjudicated by the Data Protection Board rather than through a civil suit.

An India subsidiary, branch, GCC or outsourcing vendor handling the personal data of persons in India is almost always a data fiduciary or data processor in its own right under the Act, so a transfer of that data to a foreign parent or group affiliate is a Section 16 transfer regardless of common ownership, and needs its own compliance review ahead of the 2027 deadline rather than an assumption that group membership exempts it.

sections.heading: A second compliance clock, layered on top of the first
paragraphs: A separate piece on this site has tracked the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's general compliance clock, the provisions already in force, the ones expected through November 2026, and the ones still pending. This piece narrows to two questions that sit squarely inside that clock and matter specifically to a foreign company with an India footprint: what the Act actually says about moving personal data out of the country, and what changes once a data fiduciary is designated significant. Both questions have firm statutory answers. The confusion in practice is almost always about timing, not substance, because a rule that has been notified is not the same thing as a rule that has commenced, and the 2025 Rules notified several obligations months or years before they take legal effect.

The distinction matters because a foreign parent's compliance team, reading a law-firm client alert from November 2025 describing the new Rules, can walk away with the impression that significant data fiduciary audits and cross-border traffic-data limits are a present-day obligation. They are not, not yet. But a second, equally real risk sits on the other side of that same mistake: treating the entire Rules package as a 2027 problem and ignoring the retention and governance duties that commence on a shorter fuse, or ignoring the fact that Section 16 of the Act itself, the actual transfer provision, has been in force since the Act's core provisions commenced and does not wait on the 2025 Rules at all.

This piece is written for the legal or compliance function inside a foreign company's India entity, or inside the parent's own privacy office, that needs to brief its board, its audit committee, or its parent's general counsel on exactly where the India entity stands on cross-border data movement, in terms specific enough to act on rather than a general assurance that India's data law is now in force. It deliberately stays inside the cross-border transfer and significant-data-fiduciary questions; the Act's consent architecture for ordinary, domestic processing, the rights it gives a data principal, and the breach-notification mechanics are each substantial enough to deserve separate treatment and are only touched here where they intersect directly with the questions this piece actually answers.

sections.heading: Section 16: a negative list, not a positive approval regime
paragraphs: Section 16(1) of the Act permits a data fiduciary to transfer personal data outside India to any country or territory, subject to any restriction the Central Government may notify. The structure is a negative list, not a positive one. A company does not need to find its destination country on an approved list, obtain a licence, or sign a government-approved contractual clause before transferring data abroad. It needs only to confirm that the destination has not been specifically restricted by notification. This is a materially more permissive design than the standard contractual clauses and adequacy-decision architecture a foreign company's European or UK compliance team may be used to, and it is worth stating plainly to a parent company's legal department that India's default position is permissive, because the comparison to the GDPR model is the first thing a multinational privacy team reaches for and the comparison is, on this specific point, misleading.

The qualification in Section 16(1) is doing real work, however. The Central Government can restrict transfers to a named country or territory by notification at any time, without needing a fresh Act of Parliament or amendment to the Rules. A foreign company's data-transfer map is therefore not a one-time compliance exercise completed once and filed away; a notification restricting a particular destination, issued at any point, changes the legal position for transfers to that destination going forward, and a compliance programme built around Section 16 needs a mechanism for picking up such notifications as they are issued, not an assumption that today's permissive baseline is fixed.

A second reading point worth flagging to a parent company's global privacy counsel is what Section 16 does not require. It does not ask a data fiduciary to execute a government-approved standard contractual clause before transferring data, it does not require prior notice to, or approval from, the Data Protection Board before an individual transfer, and it does not condition the transfer on the recipient jurisdiction having been assessed as providing an adequate level of protection, the test a European privacy lawyer would instinctively reach for. None of that machinery exists under the Act as presently structured. The absence of a formal adequacy or approval mechanism is sometimes described in commentary as a gap; from a compliance-planning perspective it is better understood simply as a different design choice, one that places the compliance burden on monitoring notifications rather than on securing approvals.

A third point worth separating out, because it tends to get folded into the cross-border discussion when it should not be, is that Section 16 governs where data may go, not what a data fiduciary must do with it once it gets there, and not what consent or notice the data fiduciary needed from the data principal before processing the data in the first place. Those are the Act's consent and notice obligations, which apply regardless of whether the processing happens in India or abroad and regardless of where the data is subsequently transferred. A company that has satisfied itself on the Section 16 transfer question has not, by that fact alone, also satisfied itself that it collected and processed the underlying personal data lawfully; the two questions sit side by side in the Act's structure and both need separate answers.

sections.heading: What 'restricted' means today, and why that can change without warning
paragraphs: As on the date of this article, no country or territory has been notified as restricted under Section 16(1). A data fiduciary can transfer personal data to any destination, including jurisdictions that themselves impose strict inbound controls on data from elsewhere, because the restriction runs one way, from India's side, and only by express notification. This is a meaningfully different position from the draft versions of India's data protection framework debated before the 2023 Act, several of which proposed a whitelist of approved countries, a model the final Act did not adopt.

The practical consequence for a foreign company is that a cross-border transfer lawful today under Section 16 does not carry a permanent guarantee. The mechanism for restricting a destination is a notification, not a statute, which means it can move faster than a company's annual compliance review cycle. A sensible internal control is to name a specific person or function responsible for tracking notifications issued under Section 16, in the same way a trade compliance function tracks sanctions-list updates, rather than treating the current absence of any restricted country as a permanent feature of the law.

sections.heading: The 2025 Rules and why their cross-border provisions are not live yet
paragraphs: The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025, more than two years after the parent Act received presidential assent. The Rules did not bring the entire Act into immediate operation. They set a staggered commencement structure: certain provisions, including the short title and definitions, took effect on notification; the Consent Manager framework under Rule 4 was given a twelve-month runway; and the bulk of the remaining substantive rules, reportedly including Rules 3 and 5 through 16, along with Rules 22 and 23, were given an eighteen-month runway from the notification date, placing their commencement in the middle of 2027.

Rule 13, the provision dealing with a significant data fiduciary's obligations, including the cross-border traffic-data restriction discussed below, falls within that eighteen-month group. So does Rule 8, which carries the data-retention duty discussed further on. A company's compliance timeline should therefore separate three distinct dates: the date the Act's core obligations already apply (which long predates the 2025 Rules), the Consent Manager commencement around twelve months from the Rules' notification, and the broader significant-data-fiduciary and retention obligations commencing around eighteen months from notification. Treating all three as a single 2025 or 2026 deadline, in either direction, misstates the actual compliance position.

sections.heading: Rule 13: the significant data fiduciary's cross-border traffic-data limit
paragraphs: Rule 13 gives the Central Government power to restrict a significant data fiduciary from transferring specified categories of traffic data outside India. Traffic data, in this context, is distinct from the content of a communication or transaction; it is the data generated about the fact, routing, timing and technical circumstances of processing, the kind of metadata that payment processors, telecom-adjacent platforms and large consumer internet businesses generate at volume. The restriction under Rule 13 is not a blanket localisation requirement for all personal data handled by a significant data fiduciary; it is targeted at specified categories of traffic data, and it operates alongside, not instead of, any stricter sectoral restriction that already applies under Section 16(2).

Two conditions have to be satisfied before Rule 13's cross-border limb has any practical bite on a given company. First, the company has to actually be designated a significant data fiduciary, a status conferred by government notification rather than acquired automatically by crossing a size or revenue threshold. Second, the eighteen-month commencement period for Rule 13 itself has to have run. Neither condition is met as on date for any company. A foreign-owned business that processes large volumes of Indian user data, and that expects, reasonably, to eventually be designated significant, should treat the current period as the window for getting its traffic-data classification and transfer architecture in order before either the designation or the commencement date arrives, rather than as a period in which the obligation is already live.

The distinction between traffic data and content also carries a practical engineering consequence that a legal team should flag early to its technical counterpart. Separating what the Rule actually restricts, routing, timing, device and connection metadata, from what it does not touch, the substantive content of a transaction or communication, is not always a trivial data-architecture exercise for a platform that logs the two together by default. A company that waits until designation is notified, or until Rule 13 commences, to begin that separation exercise is choosing to do under regulatory time pressure what could instead be planned calmly during the current runway, and the data-mapping work involved, identifying which systems generate traffic data, where that data currently flows, and which of those flows cross India's border, is substantially the same exercise a company would need to run for its own internal data-governance purposes regardless of what the Rule eventually requires.

sections.heading: How a company becomes a significant data fiduciary, and what follows
paragraphs: Section 10(1) of the Act lists six factors the Central Government may weigh in deciding whether to notify a data fiduciary, or a class of data fiduciaries, as significant: the volume and sensitivity of personal data processed, the risk to data principals' rights, the potential impact on India's sovereignty and integrity, the risk to electoral democracy, the risk to state security, and the risk to public order. These are assessment factors for a government notification, not a self-assessment checklist a company applies to itself. Commentary describing specific numeric thresholds, such as a stated number of users, for triggering significant status is not drawn from the statutory text and should be treated as illustrative industry guesswork rather than the legal test.

It is also worth being precise about what Section 10(1) does not say, because commercial compliance guides sometimes blur this. The provision does not list revenue, employee count, or market capitalisation as factors; it lists volume and sensitivity of personal data processed, risk to data principals' rights, and the four public-interest categories (sovereignty and integrity, electoral democracy, state security, public order). A foreign company with modest revenue in India but a very large India user base processing sensitive categories of data, health or financial information, for instance, could in principle be assessed against these factors notwithstanding a comparatively small balance sheet, while a large-revenue business processing a narrow, low-sensitivity dataset might not be. Sizing an India entity's significant-data-fiduciary risk by revenue alone, the metric a finance-led risk assessment will reach for first, therefore risks missing the actual statutory test.

Once a data fiduciary is in fact notified as significant, Section 10(2) imposes additional obligations: appointing a Data Protection Officer based in India who reports to the fiduciary's board or equivalent governing body, undertaking periodic data protection impact assessments, and arranging an independent data audit. As on date, the Central Government has not notified any data fiduciary, individually or by class, as significant. A foreign company's India entity that is large enough to plausibly attract this designation in future should build the India-based DPO function and audit trail into its medium-term compliance roadmap, but should not represent to its board, or to regulators, that it currently carries significant-data-fiduciary status or duties it has not in fact been assigned.

A related point concerns what happens before any such notification arrives. Nothing in the Act prevents a data fiduciary from voluntarily adopting significant-data-fiduciary-style governance, an India-based privacy lead, periodic internal impact assessments, an independent review of its data practices, ahead of being designated. Several multinationals operating large India businesses already run privacy governance at roughly that level as a matter of global policy, often because their other markets require it regardless of India's own designation status. For those companies, the designation question becomes largely administrative rather than operationally disruptive, since the substantive infrastructure already exists; the risk sits specifically with a company that has assumed, because no designation has issued, that no India-specific governance investment is yet warranted.

The India residency requirement for the Data Protection Officer is worth a specific note for a multinational that already runs a global or regional privacy office out of Singapore, London or elsewhere. Section 10(2) does not permit that existing global DPO, however senior or capable, to discharge the significant-data-fiduciary function for the India entity from outside the country once the designation and commencement both land; the role, as the Act frames it, has to sit with someone based in India and answerable to that entity's own board or governing body. A company that currently routes all privacy governance through a single global office should treat the possibility of future significant-data-fiduciary designation as a reason to identify, now, who within the India entity, or who it would need to hire, could step into that India-resident role, rather than leaving the question open until a notification forces an answer on a short timeline.

sections.heading: The retention duty every data fiduciary will carry, significant or not
paragraphs: Separately from the significant-data-fiduciary provisions, the 2025 Rules add a retention obligation of general application. Rule 8(3) is reported to require a data fiduciary to retain personal data, together with related traffic data and processing logs, for a period of one year, a duty that applies regardless of whether the fiduciary has been designated significant. This sits on the same eighteen-month commencement timeline as Rule 13, so it is not yet a live obligation, but it is worth distinguishing clearly from the significant-data-fiduciary provisions in internal compliance documentation, because the two are frequently bundled together in commentary despite applying to different, and overlapping, populations of companies.

For a foreign company's India operation, this retention duty intersects with ordinary data-minimisation practice in a way that needs active reconciliation rather than passive compliance. A privacy-by-design posture that deletes logs and traffic data promptly to reduce retained-data risk will need to be rebalanced against a statutory floor requiring retention for at least a year once Rule 8 commences, and the company's retention and deletion schedules should be drafted with that floor in mind well before the commencement date arrives rather than amended under time pressure once it does.

A group-level retention policy inherited from a parent company headquartered in a jurisdiction with a shorter statutory or self-imposed retention period presents the same tension in a more concrete form. If the parent's global policy instructs its India entity to purge access logs after, say, ninety days as a matter of group-wide practice, that instruction will conflict with the floor Rule 8(3) is reported to set once it commences, and the India entity cannot resolve the conflict by simply following the parent's global instruction, because the Act's obligations attach to the India entity's own processing regardless of what a foreign parent's policy prescribes. The more workable approach is to build an India-specific carve-out into the group retention policy now, rather than discover the conflict through an audit finding after the Rule has commenced.

sections.heading: Penalties, and who actually imposes them
paragraphs: The Schedule to the Act sets tiered financial penalties by category of default, enforced through the Data Protection Board of India in an adjudicatory process under Section 33, rather than through a civil suit for damages or a criminal prosecution. Reported figures place the ceiling for a failure to take reasonable security safeguards against a personal data breach, the Section 8(5) obligation, at up to Rs 250 crore, the highest tier in the Schedule. Separate tiers apply to a failure to notify the Board and affected data principals of a breach and to defaults concerning children's personal data, each reportedly capped at up to Rs 200 crore, while a breach of a significant data fiduciary's specific obligations under Section 10 is reportedly capped at up to Rs 150 crore, and a residual category covering defaults not otherwise specified in the Schedule is capped lower, at up to Rs 50 crore.

These figures come from the Schedule to the Act itself as read and summarised by multiple independent commentators, and they are worth a foreign parent company's attention for a reason that has nothing to do with the cross-border provisions discussed above: the highest exposure in the Schedule attaches to the general security-safeguards obligation under Section 8(5), which is already part of the Act's core framework and does not wait on the significant-data-fiduciary designation or the 2025 Rules' eighteen-month runway at all. A company that treats this article's cross-border and significant-data-fiduciary discussion as the whole of its DPDP exposure risks underweighting the obligation that currently carries the largest Schedule penalty.

The Data Protection Board's process is also structurally different from the civil litigation a foreign company's India legal team may be used to defending. There is no private right of action for a data principal to sue a data fiduciary directly for damages under the Act; the Board investigates and adjudicates on a complaint or reference, and the penalty, when imposed, is payable to the Government rather than to the complaining individual. This changes how a company should think about its exposure. A single aggrieved customer complaint does not, on its own, translate into the kind of class-action-style damages exposure a United States-headquartered parent might instinctively model; the realistic exposure runs through the Board's own enforcement priorities and the size of the penalty it is prepared to impose on a given finding, which is a different risk calculus from the one a litigation-trained compliance function will default to.

sections.heading: For an India subsidiary, GCC, branch or outsourcing vendor specifically
paragraphs: A foreign company often assumes that because its parent sits outside India, and because the data in question serves the parent's business in the end, the Act's transfer provisions are someone else's problem. That assumption does not survive contact with the Act's structure. An India subsidiary, branch, global capability centre or outsourcing vendor that processes the personal data of persons in India, whether its own customers' data, its own employees' data, or data it processes on behalf of an offshore client about that client's end users, is itself a data fiduciary or data processor under the Act for that data, independent of its parent's location. Moving that data to the foreign parent, to a regional data centre, or to a group-wide analytics platform hosted abroad, is a Section 16 transfer in its own right, and common ownership between the India entity and the recipient abroad does not exempt the transfer from the Act.

This matters most acutely for three structures common among foreign companies operating in India: a captive GCC processing data generated by the parent's global customer base but routing some of that processing through India-based teams; an outsourcing or BPO vendor processing a foreign client's end-customer data where some of those end customers are themselves Indian residents; and a branch or liaison office that forwards HR, vendor or customer data collected in India to a head office abroad as a matter of routine reporting. Each structure should be mapped against Section 16 and, separately, against the eventual significant-data-fiduciary and retention provisions discussed above, rather than assessed only once at entity-formation stage and left unreviewed afterward.

A fourth structure deserves its own mention because it is easy to overlook: a foreign company that has no India entity at all but processes personal data of individuals located in India in connection with offering them goods or services. Section 3 of the Act extends its reach to this processing even where it happens wholly outside India, so the absence of an India subsidiary does not, by itself, place a foreign company's direct-to-consumer business outside the framework discussed in this article, a point that a group legal function evaluating only its India-incorporated entities can miss entirely. Commentary differs on whether a second limb, reaching the profiling of individuals in India independent of any goods-or-services offering, survived in the text actually enacted, and that narrower question is best confirmed against the Gazette copy of the Act rather than assumed either way.

This fourth structure is the one most likely to be missed entirely in a group-wide compliance review, precisely because it generates no entity, no local filing, and no line item in a corporate structure chart for a parent company's general counsel to notice. An online retailer, a subscription software business, or a direct booking platform headquartered abroad and selling into India without any local incorporation can still be a data fiduciary under the Act for the Indian customers it serves, and the Section 16 transfer analysis in this article applies to that company's handling of those customers' data in exactly the same way it applies to a company that has gone to the trouble of setting up an India subsidiary. A compliance checklist organised around India entities, rather than around India-connected processing activity regardless of entity, will not catch this structure, and should be rebuilt around the latter if it currently is not.

sections.heading: Contracts, intra-group transfer and the consent manager framework, briefly
paragraphs: The Act allocates obligations between a data fiduciary and any data processor it engages through contract, and a foreign company's India entity acting as a processor for an offshore group company, or engaging an Indian processor itself, should ensure its intra-group and vendor agreements reflect that allocation rather than relying on a parent company's standard global data processing addendum drafted without reference to the Act. A transfer to a group affiliate abroad under an intra-group data-sharing agreement is still a Section 16 transfer and should be documented as such, including a record of the basis on which the destination was assessed as unrestricted at the time of transfer.

A practical difficulty many foreign companies run into is that their existing intra-group data-sharing agreement, usually drafted to satisfy a different jurisdiction's own transfer mechanism, a standard contractual clause annex or a binding corporate rules framework, says nothing at all about Section 16 or about the India entity's obligations as a fiduciary or processor under Indian law. That silence is not neutral; it leaves the India entity without a documented basis in its own compliance file showing that it considered the question at the time data started flowing. Adding an India-specific schedule or side letter to the existing group agreement, rather than waiting to draft an entirely new instrument, is usually the faster and more proportionate fix, and it gives the India entity its own paper trail independent of whatever the parent's global agreement otherwise provides for.

Separately, the Rules introduce a Consent Manager framework, a registered intermediary through which a data principal can grant, manage and withdraw consent across multiple data fiduciaries. Rule 4, which governs this framework, commences on a twelve-month timeline from the Rules' notification, shorter than the eighteen-month timeline for the significant-data-fiduciary and retention provisions. A foreign company whose India-facing consent flows are built around a parent company's global consent-management tooling should check whether that tooling needs to interoperate with a registered Consent Manager once Rule 4 commences, a question this article flags without attempting the fuller treatment it deserves on its own.

sections.heading: What remains unsettled, and what to do before 2027
paragraphs: Two significant pieces of this framework remain, deliberately, undetermined as on date. No country or territory has been notified as restricted under Section 16, and no data fiduciary has been notified as significant under Section 10. Both are matters of executive notification rather than primary legislation, and both can change at a pace a company's annual compliance review cycle may not anticipate. A compliance programme built on the assumption that today's permissive, undesignated baseline will hold indefinitely is building on sand.

The more useful posture for a foreign company's India operation, between now and the Rules' eighteen-month commencement in the middle of 2027, is to use the runway for what it is actually for: mapping every cross-border flow of personal data from the India entity, classifying which flows involve traffic data as distinct from content, assessing honestly whether the entity's scale and data sensitivity make a future significant-data-fiduciary designation plausible, and building the India-based governance functions, a DPO, an audit trail, a retention schedule consistent with Rule 8, ahead of the deadline rather than at the deadline. None of this requires waiting for the government to issue the notifications that are still outstanding; the groundwork for compliance with an obligation that is coming is not itself contingent on that obligation having commenced.

There is a narrower, year-end-specific action item worth flagging as well. A foreign company reviewing its India entity's privacy posture during its usual annual compliance cycle, which for many multinationals falls in the final quarter of the calendar year, should treat this review as the natural point to run the cross-border mapping exercise described above, rather than scheduling a separate exercise once the Rules commence. Folding this into an existing annual cycle, instead of creating a new, DPDP-specific calendar event that competes for attention with every other compliance deadline a group legal function tracks, is the more realistic way most India entities will actually get this done on time, and it avoids the common failure mode where a well-understood future obligation slips because no existing process owns the task of acting on it early.

sections.heading: Mapping the obligations against the three dates that actually matter
paragraphs: It helps to restate the timeline in a single place, because the different pieces discussed above sit on different clocks and a reader who has come this far is better served by one consolidated map than by hunting back through several sections to reconstruct it. The first date is already behind every company reading this: the Act's core obligations, including the Section 8(5) security-safeguards duty carrying the Schedule's highest penalty tier, and Section 16's negative-list transfer rule, apply now, independent of the 2025 Rules' own commencement schedule. The second date is the Consent Manager framework under Rule 4, reported to commence twelve months after the Rules' November 2025 notification, placing it around November 2026. The third date is the broader group of rules, including Rule 13's significant-data-fiduciary provisions and Rule 8's retention duty, reported to commence eighteen months after notification, placing it around the middle of 2027.

A foreign company's India compliance function gains more from treating these as three separate action items with three separate owners and three separate internal deadlines than from treating the whole package as a single DPDP project with one deadline somewhere in 2026 or 2027. The entity that has already addressed its Section 8(5) security posture, already has a view on whether its India operation's consent flows will need to interoperate with a registered Consent Manager, and has already begun the traffic-data mapping exercise described earlier in this article, will reach the middle of 2027 with genuine optionality about how it responds to whatever notification, if any, designates it significant. The entity that has treated all three as a single future problem will instead be reacting to all three at once, on a timeline it did not choose, at the point the government's own notifications finally force the question.

conclusion: India's data protection framework gives a foreign company more room on cross-border transfer than its European compliance playbook may lead it to expect, because Section 16 is a negative list and, as on date, an empty one. That room should not be mistaken for an absence of obligation. The Act's general security-safeguard duty, carrying the Schedule's highest penalty tier, is already part of the operative framework, and the significant-data-fiduciary and retention provisions in the 2025 Rules, though not yet commenced, are drafted, dated and on a fixed eighteen-month runway rather than hypothetical.

The companies best placed when that runway ends will be the ones that used it to build the compliance architecture now, India-based governance capacity, a mapped and classified data-transfer inventory, a retention schedule reconciled with Rule 8's floor, rather than the ones that waited for a government notification that may never arrive in the form expected, or that arrives faster than planned. A foreign company's India legal and compliance function is well placed to run this exercise in parallel with, rather than after, its parent's own global privacy programme, precisely because the two frameworks diverge on points, the negative list model being the clearest example, that a globally standardised playbook will not catch on its own.

faqs.q: Can an Indian company or a foreign company's India entity freely transfer personal data outside India today?
faqs.a: Yes, as a general rule. Section 16(1) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 permits transfer of personal data to any country or territory outside India unless the Central Government has specifically restricted that destination by notification. As on date, no country or territory has been so restricted, so the default position remains permissive. This can change by notification at any time, without a fresh Act of Parliament, so the position should be rechecked periodically rather than assumed to be fixed.

faqs.q: What is a significant data fiduciary, and does my company automatically qualify based on its size?
faqs.a: A significant data fiduciary is a status the Central Government confers by notification under Section 10(1) of the Act, after weighing factors including the volume and sensitivity of personal data processed and the risk to data principals' rights, India's sovereignty, electoral democracy, state security and public order. It is not a status a company acquires automatically by crossing a user count or revenue threshold, and as on date the government has not notified any data fiduciary as significant. Claims online of specific numeric thresholds for this status are not drawn from the statute.

faqs.q: When do the significant data fiduciary and cross-border traffic-data rules actually take effect?
faqs.a: The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified in November 2025 but stagger commencement. Rule 13, covering significant data fiduciary obligations including the cross-border traffic-data restriction, is reported to fall within the group of rules commencing eighteen months after notification, placing the live date around the middle of 2027. Until that date, and until a company is actually notified as significant, these specific obligations are not yet enforceable against it, though the Act's general obligations, including the security-safeguards duty, already apply.

faqs.q: Does sending data from an India subsidiary or GCC to its foreign parent count as a cross-border transfer under the Act?
faqs.a: Yes. An India subsidiary, branch or global capability centre that processes the personal data of persons in India is itself a data fiduciary or processor under the Act for that data, independent of where its parent is located. Moving that data to the foreign parent, a regional data centre, or a group analytics platform abroad is a transfer under Section 16 in its own right. Common ownership between the India entity and the recipient does not exempt the transfer from the Act's requirements.

faqs.q: What penalty can a company actually face for a data protection default in India?
faqs.a: Penalties are tiered in the Schedule to the Act and adjudicated by the Data Protection Board of India rather than awarded as civil damages. Reported ceilings place a failure to take reasonable security safeguards at up to Rs 250 crore, breach-notification and children's-data defaults at up to Rs 200 crore each, a significant data fiduciary's specific obligations at up to Rs 150 crore, and a residual, unspecified default at up to Rs 50 crore. The highest-exposure obligation, the general security-safeguards duty, is already part of the Act's operative framework.

faqs.q: Do RBI or other sector-specific data localisation rules still apply even though the DPDP Act is more permissive on cross-border transfer?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 16(2) of the Act expressly allows a sectoral law that provides a higher degree of protection or restriction on cross-border data transfer to prevail over the Act's own, more permissive, default. Payment-systems data localisation requirements, insurance-sector rules and similar sector-specific restrictions already in force are not displaced by Section 16's negative-list model, and a company has to check both frameworks rather than rely on the DPDP Act alone.

faqs.q: What should a foreign company's India operation do now, before the 2027 commencement date?
faqs.a: Use the runway to map every cross-border flow of personal data from the India entity, classify which flows involve traffic data as distinct from content, assess honestly whether the entity's scale and data sensitivity make a future significant-data-fiduciary designation plausible, and build the India-based governance capacity, a designated Data Protection Officer function, an audit trail and a retention schedule consistent with the Rules, well ahead of the commencement date rather than under time pressure once it arrives.

references: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 16(1) (transfer of personal data outside India)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 16(2) (sectoral law override)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 10(1) (factors for significant data fiduciary notification)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 10(2) (Data Protection Officer, data protection impact assessment, independent data audit)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 8(5) (reasonable security safeguards)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, Section 33 (adjudication by the Data Protection Board of India)
Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the Schedule (penalty tiers)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 1 (short title and commencement)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 4 (Consent Manager; twelve-month commencement)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 8(3) (retention of personal data, traffic data and processing logs; reported figure)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rule 13 (significant data fiduciary obligations and cross-border traffic-data restriction)
Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, Rules 3 and 5 to 16, 22 and 23 (reported eighteen-month commencement group)
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology, notification of the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, November 2025
verification_notes: AUDIENCE: foreign company. TARGET QUERY: does the DPDP Act let a foreign company move Indian personal data abroad, what is a significant data fiduciary, when do the DPDP Rules 2025 cross-border provisions take effect. DEMAND EVIDENCE: no search-volume tool was used; this is a live, frequently discussed compliance question across law-firm client alerts following the November 2025 notification of the Rules, and the combination of the cross-border transfer rule with the significant-data-fiduciary timeline, aimed specifically at a foreign company's India subsidiary or GCC, had not previously been covered in this set of articles (the earlier DPDP compliance-clock article covers the Act's general timeline rather than this specific cross-border and SDF angle). Section 16's negative-list structure and the sectoral override in Section 16(2) are confirmed from multiple independent sources (Taxmann, King Stubb & Kasiva, miniOrange, and the dpdpa.com text aggregator), all converging on the same mechanism; this research relied on secondary aggregation of the statutory text rather than the official Gazette copy, since WebFetch to government and primary-source domains was not reachable in this session's network configuration, and the article is written accordingly as a secondary-source-confirmed account rather than one checked against the India Code or Gazette text directly. The absence of any country currently restricted under Section 16 and of any entity currently notified as a significant data fiduciary is reported consistently across the sources reviewed, with one commentary piece (a Substack-style post) specifically noting the point for cross-border restriction and a separate Taxmann-affiliated commentary (ksandk.com) making the same point for SDF designation; this research treats the absence as the current position but flags in the article itself that it can change by notification without warning. The November 2025 notification date for the Rules is confirmed by multiple sources (SSRana, Hogan Lovells/CA, AMSShardul, Cyril Shroff/CAM client alert) but these sources differ on whether the specific day was 13 or 14 November 2025; this article therefore states only the month, not the day, consistent with the instruction to state only what sources agree on. The staggered commencement structure, twelve months for the Consent Manager under Rule 4 and eighteen months for the bulk of the remaining rules including the group described as Rules 3 and 5 to 16, 22 and 23, is confirmed from Bar & Bench's enumeration of the commencement groups; a second source (the AMSShardul regulatory alert) corroborates the general three-tier staggered structure and the Consent Manager's twelve-month placement, though this research did not find a second source independently reproducing the full numbered list of rules in the eighteen-month group, so the specific inclusion of Rule 13 and Rule 8 in that group is stated on the strength of Bar & Bench's enumeration read together with Hogan Lovells/CA's and SFLC's independent descriptions of Rule 13's eighteen-month-aligned, not-yet-commenced status, which corroborate the substance (that Rule 13 is not yet in force and sits on the longer timeline) even though they do not each independently re-derive the full numbered list. Rule 13's restriction on a significant data fiduciary's cross-border transfer of specified traffic data is confirmed from two independent sources (Bar & Bench and Hogan Lovells/CA), both converging on the same mechanism and the traffic-data (rather than all personal data) scope. Rule 8(3)'s one-year retention requirement for personal data, traffic data and processing logs is sourced primarily from a single named reference (S&R Associates, as reported in an aggregated search result) for the specific rule number, with a second source (Lakshmikumaran & Sridharan, similarly reported) corroborating the general obligation's existence and its application to all data fiduciaries rather than only significant ones; this research treats the general obligation as two-source confirmed and flags the specific sub-rule numbering as resting on a single clear attribution, consistent with the instruction to state facts no more firmly than the sources support. Section 10(1)'s six listed factors for significant data fiduciary designation are confirmed from the dpdpa.com statutory-text aggregator together with Taxmann's commentary, both converging on the same six factors and on designation being a government notification rather than a self-assessed threshold; the specific numeric user-count thresholds appearing in some commercial guides are explicitly identified in the sources themselves as illustrative rather than statutory, and this article states that caveat rather than repeating an unconfirmed figure. The Schedule penalty tiers, up to Rs 250 crore for a Section 8(5) security-safeguards default, up to Rs 200 crore for breach-notification and children's-data defaults, up to Rs 150 crore for significant-data-fiduciary obligation breaches, and up to Rs 50 crore residually, are confirmed from multiple independent sources (Bar & Bench, Telangana Today, and a King Stubb & Kasiva analysis aggregating a Data Guidance infographic), all converging on the same four figures and their respective triggers, while one additional source's claim of a Rs 500 crore maximum and another's conflicting Rs 200 crore figure for the security-safeguards tier were identified as outliers inconsistent with the converging sources and are not relied upon. Nothing in this article relies on an invented section number, rule number, case citation or figure; every figure and commencement date carries the hedging the underlying source material actually supports, and the article explicitly flags the two points, the restricted-country list and the significant-data-fiduciary designation, that remain open as on date.
